title: Cooling Cities with Tree Canopies
body: A. Urban planners have long planted trees for aesthetic reasons, but recent heatwaves have shifted attention toward their practical role in cooling streets. Leaves intercept solar radiation, while water released through transpiration removes heat from the surrounding air. The effect is strongest where mature trees form a connected canopy rather than isolated patches.

B. However, the relationship between trees and temperature is not simple. Dense planting can reduce airflow in narrow streets, trapping pollutants close to the ground. Species choice also matters: trees with high water demand may be unsuitable for dry regions, especially when cities rely on limited reservoirs.

C. Several councils now use thermal images and street-level sensors to identify neighbourhoods with both high temperatures and low canopy cover. These areas are often socially disadvantaged, so planting programmes increasingly consider equity as well as average city temperature.

D. Researchers caution that planting targets alone are inadequate. Young trees provide little shade and many fail during their first three years because of poor soil, vandalism, or insufficient watering. Long-term maintenance budgets may therefore matter more than the number of saplings announced at the beginning of a programme.

title: Handwritten Notes and Digital Recall
body: A. Students who write notes by hand often record fewer words than students using laptops. This apparent disadvantage can encourage them to select and reorganise information rather than copy a lecture word for word.

B. Some experiments report better conceptual recall among handwriting groups, but the results are not universal. Differences in prior knowledge, typing speed, and study habits can influence performance, and many studies involve short laboratory tasks rather than an entire course.

C. Digital notes offer benefits that are difficult to reproduce on paper. They can be searched, reorganised, linked to readings, and shared with classmates. They also support students who cannot write quickly or who use accessibility software.

D. The most useful distinction may not be between paper and screens, but between passive transcription and active processing. A student who types a concise summary and later tests themselves may learn more than someone who fills pages by hand without reviewing them.

title: The Expanding Night
body: A. Artificial light has extended productive and recreational hours, yet it has also transformed the natural night. Satellite measurements show that illuminated areas are expanding in many regions, even where energy-efficient lamps have replaced older bulbs.

B. One reason is the rebound effect. Because modern LEDs are cheaper to operate, organisations may install more fixtures or increase brightness. Savings per lamp do not necessarily produce lower total electricity use.

C. Ecologists are particularly concerned about insects. Many species navigate using celestial light and can become trapped around lamps, where they exhaust themselves or become easy prey. Changes in insect abundance can then affect plants, birds, and other animals.

D. Solutions do not require cities to become completely dark. Shielding fixtures, reducing blue wavelengths, dimming lights during quiet hours, and illuminating only places that need it can all reduce ecological damage while preserving safety.

title: Repair Cafes and the Culture of Maintenance
body: A. Repair cafes are community events where volunteers help visitors fix household objects. The concept began as a response to waste, but organisers soon noticed that the events also transferred practical knowledge and reduced the isolation of some participants.

B. Electrical items are among the most common objects brought to these events. A broken cable or worn switch can sometimes be replaced cheaply, although volunteers must refuse repairs when an appliance is unsafe or requires specialist certification.

C. Clothing repairs usually have a high success rate because the necessary tools are simple and replacement material is inexpensive. Furniture can be more difficult, as large items are hard to transport and may require long periods of work.

D. Critics point out that occasional events cannot by themselves reverse a disposable economy. Products may be sealed, spare parts may be unavailable, and manufacturers may not publish repair instructions. Supporters therefore argue that repair cafes should be combined with stronger product-design rules and consumer rights.
